title: Ecosystems, Bioaccumulation and Invasive Species
kicker: Cambridge Lower Secondary · Science 0893 · Stage 8 · Biology
summary: Ecosystems around the Earth and the habitats inside them, how toxic substances build up along food chains, and how invasive species such as water hyacinth change whole ecosystems — with food-web practice in Checkpoint style.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Identify different ecosystems on the Earth and recognise that one ecosystem contains many different habitats (8Be.01)
Describe how toxic substances build up in living things (bioaccumulation) and the effect this has on an ecosystem (8Be.02)
Describe how a new or invasive species can affect other organisms and the whole ecosystem (8Be.03)

blocks.text: An **ecosystem** is all the living organisms in an area **together with** the non-living (physical) environment they live in, and all the ways they **interact**. The organisms depend on each other (for food, shelter, pollination) and on the non-living parts (water, light, temperature, soil, air). Because everything is linked, a change to one part — a poison in the water, or a new animal arriving — can affect the whole ecosystem.

blocks.text: Ecosystems on the Earth

Ecosystems come in all sizes. The Red Sea coral reef is a huge ecosystem; a pond, a rotting log or even a school garden is a small one. Each ecosystem has its own conditions, and the organisms living there are adapted to them.

rows: **Hot desert**
Egypt's Western Desert (Sahara)
Very dry; very hot days and cold nights
camel, fennec fox, scorpion, desert lizard, acacia tree
sand dunes, under rocks, burrows, oases, rocky hills
**Coral reef**
Red Sea (e.g. Ras Mohammed)
Warm, clear, shallow, salty water; lots of light
corals, parrotfish, clownfish, sea turtles, sharks
reef crest, caves and cracks, seagrass beds, sandy sea floor, open water
**Fresh water (river and lake)**
The Nile; Lake Nasser
Fresh water; muddy bottom; reeds at the edges
tilapia, Nile perch, crocodile, heron, reeds
river bank, reed beds, open water, muddy bottom
**Tropical rainforest**
Amazon (South America), Congo (Africa)
Hot and wet all year
monkeys, parrots, frogs, insects, tall trees
canopy (tree tops), forest floor, rivers, under bark
**Grassland (savannah)**
East Africa
Grasses, few trees; a wet season and a dry season
zebra, lion, termites, acacia
open grass, termite mounds, waterholes
**Polar**
Arctic, Antarctica
Very cold; ice and snow; long dark winters
polar bear (Arctic), penguin (Antarctica), seals
sea ice, open sea, under the ice
**Deep ocean**
Ocean floor far below the surface
Dark, cold, very high pressure
deep-sea fish, squid, worms
ocean floor, hot-water vents

blocks.text: **One ecosystem, many habitats.** Inside a single ecosystem there are many different places to live, each with slightly different conditions. Different organisms live in each one.

blocks.text: **Microhabitats** are tiny habitats: under a stone in the desert (cool and damp for a scorpion), inside a crack in a coral, under the bark of a tree. **Exam tip:** an ecosystem includes the non-living environment; a habitat is just the place where an organism lives.

blocks.title: النظام البيئي والموطن
blocks.text: النظام البيئي (ecosystem) = كل الكائنات الحية في منطقة + البيئة غير الحية (مياه، ضوء، حرارة، تربة) والعلاقة بينهم. الموطن (habitat) = المكان اللي الكائن عايش فيه. النظام البيئي الواحد فيه مواطن كتير: الشعاب المرجانية في البحر الأحمر فيها حشائش البحر، والكهوف والشقوق، والمية المفتوحة، والقاع الرملي.
Food chains and food webs: a quick reminder

Feeding links join the organisms of an ecosystem. In a **food chain**, the arrow means **"is eaten by"** and shows the direction energy (and anything in the food) moves. A **producer** (a plant or alga) makes its own food; **consumers** eat other organisms. The animal at the end of the chain is the **top predator**. A **food web** shows many food chains linked together. Because of these links, anything that changes one population affects others — and anything that is in the food (including poisons) is passed along the chain.
Bioaccumulation of toxic substances

Some toxic substances get into ecosystems from human activities: **pesticides** (such as DDT, used in the past to kill insects), **heavy metals** such as **mercury** and **lead** from factories and mining, and some industrial chemicals. The dangerous ones share two properties:

items: They are **not broken down** easily in the environment — they last for many years.
When an organism takes them in, its body **cannot break them down or get rid of them**, so they are **stored** (often in fat) and **build up** over its life. This is **bioaccumulation**.

blocks.caption: A pesticide in a lake. The concentration in the water is tiny, but it increases at every step of the food chain. The fish-eating bird (top predator) has the highest concentration.

items: Tiny amounts of the pesticide wash into the water, and **plankton** (tiny organisms) take it in. It stays in their bodies.
Each **small fish** eats **many** plankton over its life. It keeps all the pesticide from all of them, so its concentration is higher.
Each **large fish** eats many small fish, and each **fish-eating bird** eats many large fish. At every step the pesticide becomes **more concentrated**.
So **top predators** have the **highest** concentration — high enough to harm or kill them, even though the water seemed only slightly polluted.

blocks.text: The impact on an ecosystem

rows: Top predators are **poisoned** — they become ill, die, or cannot **reproduce**

In the 1950s–60s, DDT built up in birds of prey such as peregrine falcons and eagles. It made them lay eggs with **thin shells** that broke when the parents sat on them, so few chicks hatched and their populations fell sharply. Many countries then banned DDT, and the birds slowly recovered.
**Humans** can be harmed — we are often top consumers

In Minamata, Japan (1950s), a factory released mercury compounds into the bay. Mercury built up in fish and shellfish, and people and cats that ate them were badly poisoned. Today pregnant women are often advised to limit large predatory fish such as swordfish, which can contain more mercury.
**Knock-on effects** through the food web

If the top predator population falls, the animals it ate may increase in number; they then eat more of their own food, so that population may fall. The balance of the whole ecosystem changes and **biodiversity** can fall.

blocks.text: **How to reduce bioaccumulation:** ban or limit long-lasting pesticides; use pesticides that break down quickly or biological pest control; treat factory waste before it reaches rivers and seas; test fish for mercury.
**Exam technique — calculations:** "How many times greater?" means **divide** the bigger concentration by the smaller one. For example, bird ÷ small fish = 25 ÷ 0.5 = **50 times**.
New and invasive species

A **native species** lives naturally in an area. Sometimes a **new species** arrives that has never lived there. Humans often bring them — on purpose (as pets, farm animals, garden plants, fish for fishing, or to control pests) or by accident (in ships' ballast water, on cargo, through canals). Many new species die out or fit in without harm. But some become **invasive**: they **spread quickly** and **harm** native species and the ecosystem.

headers: Why invasive species spread so quickly
How they affect other organisms and the ecosystem
rows: **No natural predators** or diseases in the new area (these were left behind in their home area)
**Competition**: they compete with native species for food, space, light or nesting sites, and often win, so native populations fall
They **reproduce quickly** and in large numbers
**Predation**: they eat native species that have no defences against them
They are good **competitors** and can live in many conditions
**Disease**: they can bring diseases that kill native species
Native animals may not eat them (they may be poisonous or unfamiliar)
**Habitat change**: they can change the habitat itself (e.g. covering water, blocking light)
**Food web effects**: changes in one population pass along the web; **biodiversity** falls; some native species may become **extinct**

blocks.text: Case studies

rows: **Water hyacinth** in the Nile and Egyptian canals
A floating plant from South America, spread as a garden pond plant

Grows extremely fast and covers the water surface → **blocks light**, so water plants and algae below die → when they rot, microorganisms use up the **oxygen**, so **fish die**. It also blocks irrigation canals and boats, and loses a lot of water from its leaves.
**Nile perch** in Lake Victoria (East Africa)
Put into the lake in the 1950s to give fishermen a large fish to catch
A large predator with no predators of its own in the lake; it ate huge numbers of small native **cichlid** fish, and many of the hundreds of cichlid species disappeared.
**Cane toad** in Australia
Brought in 1935 to eat beetles that damaged sugar cane
It did not control the beetles, but bred quickly and spread over a huge area. Its skin is **poisonous**, so native predators (snakes, lizards, quolls) that eat it **die**.
**Lionfish** in the Caribbean and western Atlantic
Native to the Red Sea and Indian Ocean; released from home aquariums
No predators there; it eats huge numbers of small reef fish, so reef fish populations fall.
**Grey squirrel** in Britain
Brought from North America
**Out-competes** the native red squirrel for food and carries a disease that kills red squirrels; red squirrels have disappeared from most of England.

blocks.text: **Controlling invasive species:** prevention is best (checking ships and cargo, never releasing pets or aquarium fish into the wild). Others are removed by hand or machine (water hyacinth is cut and lifted out of canals), or controlled by a carefully tested natural enemy — for example, small weevils that eat only water hyacinth have been used in some lakes.

blocks.text: **How to answer food web questions about a new species:** (1) find what the new species **eats** — those populations will **decrease**; (2) find which animals **ate the same food** — they now face **competition** and may decrease; (3) follow the arrows **one more step** — the food of the animals that decreased may now **increase**. Always give the **reason** for each change.

blocks.title: التراكم الحيوي والأنواع الغازية
blocks.text: التراكم الحيوي: مادة سامة (زي مبيد DDT أو الزئبق) ما بتتكسرش وما بتخرجش من الجسم، فبتتخزن. وكل حيوان بياكل كتير من اللي قبله في السلسلة الغذائية، فالتركيز بيزيد في كل خطوة، وأعلى تركيز بيكون في المفترس الأخير (زي الطيور اللي بتاكل سمك). النوع الغازي: كائن جديد اتنقل لمكان مش مكانه، ومالوش أعداء طبيعيين هناك، فبيتكاثر بسرعة وينافس أو ياكل الأنواع المحلية — زي ورد النيل اللي بيغطي المية ويمنع الضوء فالسمك يموت.
Worked examples

**Worked example 1** (ecosystem or habitat?)
(a) Explain the difference between an ecosystem and a habitat. [2]
(b) Name two different habitats within a coral reef ecosystem. [1]

items: (a) An ecosystem is **all the organisms** in an area **and their physical (non-living) environment**, interacting [1]; a habitat is **the place where an organism lives** [1].
(b) Any two: seagrass bed, reef crest, caves / cracks in the coral, open water, sandy sea floor, reef slope.
**Common mistake:** naming another ecosystem ("desert") when the question asks for a habitat **within** the reef.

blocks.text:
**Worked example 2** (bioaccumulation calculation)
Use the pesticide diagram above.
(a) How many times greater is the concentration in the large fish than in the plankton? [1]
(b) Explain why the fish-eating bird has the highest concentration. [2]

items: (b) The pesticide is **not broken down / not excreted**, so it stays in the body [1]; each bird **eats many fish** over its life, so it takes in the pesticide from all of them and it **builds up** to a high concentration [1].
**Common mistake:** "The bird drinks the polluted water." The water concentration is tiny; nearly all the pesticide comes from **food**.

blocks.text:
**Worked example 3** (impact on an ecosystem)
A farmer sprays a long-lasting pesticide near a river. Twenty years later there are far fewer kingfishers (fish-eating birds) along the river. Suggest how the pesticide caused this and one other effect on the river ecosystem. [3]

items: The pesticide washed into the river and **built up along the food chain** (bioaccumulation) [1].
Kingfishers, as **top predators**, got the highest concentration, so many **died or could not breed** (e.g. thin eggshells) [1].
Other effect: with fewer kingfishers, the **number of small fish may increase**, so the animals they eat (e.g. insect larvae) may decrease / the balance of the food web changes [1].

blocks.text:
**Worked example 4** (invasive species in a food web)
Use the lake food web above. The introduced fish spreads quickly.
(a) Suggest what happens to the number of small fish. Explain your answer. [2]
(b) Explain why the number of herons may fall. [2]
(c) Suggest what may happen to the algae. Explain your answer. [2]

items: (a) Small fish **decrease** [1], because the introduced fish **eats** them (and it has no predators in the lake) [1].

(b) The heron also eats small fish, so there is **less food** for it / it **competes** with the introduced fish [1]; herons may eat more frogs, so frogs decrease too, and some herons starve or move away [1].
(c) Algae may **increase** [1], because fewer small fish and insect larvae are left to **eat** the algae [1].
**Exam technique:** use the word **because**, and name the organisms from the web.

blocks.text:
**Worked example 5** (water hyacinth)
Water hyacinth covers the surface of a canal. Explain why fish in the canal die. [3]

items: The plant **blocks light** from reaching water plants and algae below. [1]
They cannot photosynthesise, so they die and **rot**; the microorganisms that decompose them **use up oxygen** (and less oxygen is made by photosynthesis). [1]
The fish do not get enough **oxygen** for respiration, so they die. [1]

blocks.text:
**Worked example 6** (why invasive species spread)
Suggest two reasons why cane toads spread so quickly across Australia. [2]

items: Any two: **no natural predators** in Australia (predators that eat them die because the toads are poisonous); **no diseases** to control them; they **reproduce quickly** / lay many eggs; plenty of food; they can live in many habitats.
**Common mistake:** "because they are invasive" — that just repeats the question.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Mixing up **ecosystem** (living + non-living, interacting) and **habitat** (the place an organism lives).
Saying the top predator gets poisoned because it "drinks the water". It gets the poison from the **many organisms it eats**.
Forgetting to say the substance is **not broken down or excreted** — that is why it builds up.
Writing "the population will change" without saying **increase or decrease** and **why**.
Thinking every new species is invasive. A species is invasive only if it **spreads and causes harm**.
Reading food web arrows backwards. The arrow points **to the eater**.
In "how many times" questions, subtracting instead of **dividing**.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: **Food web questions**: "An invasive species is added. Describe and explain what happens to population X." Give the change (increase/decrease) **and** the reason from the web.
**Bioaccumulation data**: a diagram or table of concentrations along a food chain. Calculate "how many times greater" and explain why the top predator has the most.
**Match** ecosystems to their conditions, or **identify habitats** within one ecosystem from a picture.
**Suggest** reasons: why an invasive species spreads (no predators, fast reproduction) or why a toxic substance is dangerous (not broken down).
**Evaluate**: "Was introducing species X a good idea?" Give an advantage and a disadvantage and reach a conclusion.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Ecosystems, bioaccumulation and invasive species: practice
blocks.intro: 14 Checkpoint-style questions, from easy to hard. Use the food web and the data. Full solutions are given after you check your answers.

questions.q: Which of these is the best description of an ecosystem?
c: the place where one organism lives
all the animals of one species in an area
all the living organisms in an area together with their non-living environment, interacting
a list of the producers in an area
questions.e: An ecosystem includes the living organisms AND the non-living (physical) environment and how they interact. The place where an organism lives is a habitat; all of one species is a population.

questions.q: What is the name for the place where an organism lives?
questions.e: A habitat is the place where an organism lives. One ecosystem contains many habitats.

questions.q: Which of these is a habitat WITHIN a coral reef ecosystem?
questions.e: Cracks and caves in the coral are habitats within the reef (for eels, octopus). A sand dune is a desert habitat; a rainforest is a different ecosystem; sea ice is in polar ecosystems.

questions.q: A pesticide that is not broken down gets into a food chain. Which organism will have the highest concentration of pesticide in its body?
questions.e: The pesticide builds up at each step because each animal eats many organisms from the level below. The top predator, at the end of the chain, has the highest concentration.

questions.p:
Question 5
Scientists measured the concentration of mercury in organisms in a sea food chain:
algae → shrimp → small fish → tuna
Organism | Mercury concentration in μg per g
algae | 0.02
shrimp | 0.1
small fish | 0.6
tuna | 3.0
questions.q: (a) How many times greater is the mercury concentration in the tuna than in the shrimp?

questions.p:
Question 5
Scientists measured the concentration of mercury in organisms in a sea food chain:
algae → shrimp → small fish → tuna
Organism | Mercury concentration in μg per g
algae | 0.02
shrimp | 0.1
small fish | 0.6
tuna | 3.0
questions.q: (b) Explain why the concentration of mercury is highest in the tuna. [2]
questions.ms: 1 mark: mercury is not broken down / not excreted, so it stays (is stored) in the body. 1 mark: the tuna eats many small fish (each containing mercury), so the mercury builds up / accumulates. Accept: tuna is the top predator, at the end of the food chain, with mercury passed along the chain (max 1 without the 'many' idea).
questions.e: Mercury is not broken down or removed by the body, so it stays in each organism's tissues. A tuna eats a very large number of small fish over its life and keeps the mercury from all of them, so mercury builds up to the highest concentration in the tuna, the top predator.

questions.q: What is the scientific name for the build-up of a toxic substance in an organism and along a food chain?
questions.e: Bioaccumulation: the toxic substance builds up in the organism because it is not broken down or excreted, and its concentration increases along the food chain (this increase is also called biomagnification).

questions.q: Why do many invasive species spread very quickly in a new area?
c: They are always larger than native species
They have no natural predators or diseases there
They cannot reproduce in the new area
Native species help them to find food
questions.e: Their natural predators and diseases were left behind in their home area, so nothing controls their numbers and they reproduce and spread fast.

questions.q: (c) The introduced fish spreads quickly. Suggest what will happen to the number of frogs. Explain your answer. [2]
questions.ms: 1 mark: a prediction — frogs decrease (most likely). 1 mark: a reason linked to the food web — the introduced fish eats insect larvae, so frogs have less food (competition); OR herons have fewer small fish, so they eat more frogs. Also accept 'frogs increase' for both marks ONLY if clearly explained (e.g. the fish eats the small fish that compete with frogs for larvae, so frogs get more food).
questions.e: The number of frogs will probably decrease. The introduced fish eats insect larvae, which are the frogs' food, so there is less food for frogs. Also, the introduced fish eats small fish, so herons have fewer small fish to eat and are likely to eat more frogs.

questions.q: Water hyacinth covers the surface of a lake. Explain why the number of fish in the lake falls. [3]
questions.ms: 1 mark: it blocks light from reaching plants/algae under the water. 1 mark: they cannot photosynthesise / they die and rot; decomposers use up oxygen / less oxygen is produced. 1 mark: fish do not get enough oxygen (for respiration) and die. Accept also: less food for fish because plants/algae die (max 1 in place of the oxygen idea).
questions.e: The water hyacinth stops light reaching the water plants and algae below. They cannot photosynthesise, so they die and are decomposed by microorganisms that use up oxygen from the water (and no new oxygen is made). The fish cannot get enough oxygen for respiration, so many die.

questions.q: In the past, the pesticide DDT built up in birds of prey. What effect did this have on these birds?
c: They laid more eggs than normal
They became immune to all diseases
They laid eggs with thin shells that broke easily
questions.e: DDT built up in birds of prey and made their eggshells thin. The eggs broke during incubation, so few chicks hatched and the populations fell.

questions.q: A species that lives naturally in an area, and was not brought there by humans, is called a ______ species.
questions.e: Native (indigenous) species live naturally in an area. A species brought from somewhere else that spreads and causes harm is an invasive species.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Ecosystem = living organisms + their non-living environment, interacting. Habitat = the place where an organism lives. One ecosystem has many habitats.
Examples of ecosystems: desert, coral reef, river or lake, rainforest, grassland, polar, deep ocean.
Bioaccumulation: a toxic substance that is not broken down or excreted builds up in an organism; its concentration increases at each step of a food chain, so top predators are harmed most.
Invasive species spread fast (no predators or diseases, fast breeding) and harm natives by competition, predation and disease; effects pass through the food web and biodiversity falls.
In food web questions, always state increase or decrease AND give the reason using the feeding links.
